॥ Commentary on the *Prāsāda-ṣaṭślokī* ॥
(side heading) (Hariḥ Oṃ: Commentary on the Prāsāda Verses) Commentary on the Prāsāda Verses.

O Lord of the Assembly of Embodiments, by a mere fragment of Your grace, I now compose this commentary on the *Ṣaṭślokī* of the venerable *Prāsāda*. (l. 2) ...For indeed, the *hauṃ*-syllable, which constitutes the five-syllabled seed-mantra (*bīja*) denoting Paramaśiva, is described in manifold ways within the Śiva Āgamas through its divisions into three, five, eight, nine, and sixteen *kalās*; therein [is found] the twelve-*kalā* *Prāsāda*... (l. 4) "In the paths of space, time, and the fingers, known as the Great Cause (*mahākāraṇa*), who indeed—having understood the pervasion of the *kalās* by Śakti and Kṛtya... (l. 5)

Having thus described [the temple] primarily as having twelve kalās, the Teacher—[omitting the rest of his name]—describes the source of the syllable *akāra* and its radiance with half a verse, while illustrating the temple of twelve kalās through six verses. "From the root, from the world that is the abode of Kuṇḍalinī, Śiva, resembling a peacock, dwells within the navel, possessing a luster for a moment like a vowel-sound (*mātra*) amidst the consonants (*hal*). From that root-lotus, the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, he has arisen"—this is the ellipsis.
[He possesses] the sound of a swan (*marālasvana*)... [and so forth].
The initial flash of light is like the sudden emergence of lightning. The mere consonant *ha*, devoid of vowel, is Śiva; it is the seed of Śiva. It remains until the end of knowledge (*jñāvadhi*).

Below it, the Kuṇḍalinī power revolves, following after *māyā* and *karman*. Since it is stated that "the effects such as *nāda* and *bindu* belong to her as well," and because of the statement regarding the stability of the world, it is established—just as with cotton and other materials—that even the seed of Śiva is produced by the Kuṇḍalinī power.

Because [the sound] of the subtle resonance (*sūkṣmanāda*) is heard by those whose auditory canals have been severed [of external noise] and whose minds are concentrated, its status as an internal sound is established. Because of its connection with the *medhākalā* to be described later, it is merely a manifestation (*vyañjana*). The usage of *mātra* in *halmātra* is employed [in this sense].
The reading *kṛto halmātraśaśivaḥ* is easily understood; for there is no [perception] of a person without sound. ...pra...

From the statement "How by that? it is established that its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*) by virtue of being an awakener; thus, its quality of possessing the brilliance of lightning is proven, and not [the state of] *nābhyanta* due to the restriction of its location. (l. 7) ...There is no such restriction of location for that which has dissolved; however, for that which is conjoined [with the breath], the intention is that it extends as far as the *brahmarandhra*.

Now, regarding the measure of the digit of intelligence (*medhākalā*), the space of the feet of the *īśvara-nāda*—(l. 8) ...by three quarters of the *tattva*, there is an oblation (*āhuti*). Above that, on a foot that leaps a span (*vitasti*), there are four [fingers]... (p. 5b, l. 1)

The fruit... he obtains above the radiance of the flame of fire, through the wisdom of the four hundred principles (*tattva*s). Thus, O Lord, the Blessed One seated upon the lotus [attains] this for the twenty-four [principles]. In this very context, the application of the words is as follows: above that, by leaping a span (*vitasti*) onto the foot, one reaches the heart-lotus; there is a trident (*śūla*) with four [spikes], and above that, by leaping and not leaping, one obtains the wisdom of the radiance of the flame of fire of the four hundred principles. O Lord, the Blessed One seated upon the lotus [is the master of this].

Below that [seat], which is not reaching the navel-lotus, at a distance of two *vitastis* above—that is, having stepped forward by twenty finger-breadths—at the place of the feet, the heart-cavity (*hṛtkanda*), the heart-lotus, measures four finger-breadths; above that, in its upper portion, there is the radiance of the crest of fire, surging with three *mātrās*.

The flame of the lamp’s fire reaches as far as the intellect (*medhā*); likewise, the crescent of the letter *au* reaches and abides [there]. Regarding the twenty-four principles (*tattva*)—from the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*) beginning with earth—the Lord Brahmā, seated upon the lotus, [is reached] by means of the letter *na*, the Lord without cause (*akāraṇeśvara*). Starting from the navel-lotus, the letter *ha*, accompanied by the intellect (*medhā*), reaches as far as the heart-lotus; this is the intended meaning. Now, the second verse:

With the second and third feet, he describes the entire hand: marked by two measures (*mātrā*), it possesses the light of the moon, the sun, and fire, along with the six desired syllables (*iṣṭāṅgula*) in the throat;
[this is] the Person (*pumān*) accompanied by Lakṣmī, together with the six principles (*tattva*) mentioned in the *Śruti*.

Herein is the construction of the words regarding this meaning: "In the neck, eight finger-breadths [from the heart], the light of the moon and the sun..."—the word "ear" (*śruti*) is to be supplied as the remainder. And of that [neck], there is the Lord, the Person accompanied by Lakṣmī, conjoined with the six principles (*tattva*); thus, the preceding words are to be supplied. But below, starting from the heart-lotus, it extends for eight finger-breadths.

In the region extending up to the throat, there is the luster of the moon and the sun—the radiance of the moon and the sun-stone; it is marked by two measures (*mātrā*), meaning it is endowed with two *mātrās*. It is the letter *Ā*, which is the end of the Veda (*śruti*); "the end of the Veda" refers to the right ear, and its terminus is the letter *Ū*, situated at the location of the left ear. This is accompanied by the six principles (*tattva*) and the [six] digits (*kalā*).

In the principles (tattvas) known as Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, and Puruṣa, accompanied by the group of six (the Kalās), and joined with Lakṣmī because he effects maintenance (sthiti), the Person (Pumān)—who is the cause of protection and endowed with exalted glory—is the agent called "Worship" (Nārādhana), the Lord of Causes. The sense is that [this energy] moves upward from the heart-lotus to the end of the throat.

Now, by the fourth quarter of the second verse and the first quarter of the third verse, he describes the "uneven digit" (viṣamakalā): one should remember the uneven digit marked by a measure of four finger-breadths on the tongue, which has the luster of a lightning-streak, and is Hara accompanied by Māyā, whose abode is the cremation ground (pitṛvana).

In this very context, the following is said: "On the tongue, which measures four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), marked by a single measure (*ekamātrā*) beginning from the root of the throat and extending to the root of the tongue, possessing the brilliant luster of a fierce lightning flash, one should remember Hara—the poison-seed of the world, whose companion is Māyā, and who dwells in the cremation ground. The meaning is as follows: on the tongue measuring four finger-breadths, starting from the base of the throat, there is a mark of a single measure (*ekamātrā*) at the limit of the root of the tongue.

She whose luster is like a garland of lightning flashes of limited duration; she who possesses such radiance—she is thus described. She made the cremation ground (pitṛvana), which is the world (jagat)—that is, the cremation ground of the worlds beyond the universe—the domain of Rudra, having performed the act of dissolution.

Thus it is said that the world consists of the ancestors (pitṛmaya). In the reading "sakalalokapitṛsvarūpamāyāsahāyam," it means having Māyā as her companion—that is, having Māyā, the deluder, as her assistant or collaborator. By the phrase "māyāsahāya," it should be understood that the principle of Māyā is the single principle within the portion of poison (viṣakalā); thus one should remember Hara, that is, Rudra.
The meaning of "one should sustain" (*dhāyayet*) is that one should contemplate the letter *A* starting from the root of the throat up to the root of the tongue.

Now, by means of the second and third quarters of the third verse, he describes the *bindu-kalā*: "There, between the two eyebrows, at a distance of two fingers, is the lamp-like [point]... joined with the two principles (*dvitatva*) and endowed with the duration of a *mātrā*, it is the *bindu* of the arms of Vidyā.

In this regard, the application of the words is as follows: there, in the space of two finger-breadths between the eyebrows, one should meditate upon the *bindu-vidyā*—which is conjoined with the sense of being the size of a lamp-flame, which is expanded, and which is presided over by the arms—as the specific distinction. There, the tongue... [is] two finger-breadths [in length].

In the space between the eyebrows, measured by two finger-breadths—that is, limited to the middle of the brow—one finds the point (*bindu*), which possesses half of the pale white radiance of a lamp flame rivaling the wick of the sacrificial fire; it is measured by a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), joined with the two *tattvas*, and conjoined with both Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara. It is the *bindu* and the *bindukalā*.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon it as presided over by the Great Lords who enjoy the Vidyās. (l. 5) The intention is that one should meditate on the mass of *bindu*-kalās from the root of the palate up to the middle of the eyebrows. Now, with the fourth line of the third verse, he describes the *ardhacandra*-kalā: "...furthermore, [it is] beautiful as a half-moon, marked by a single foot-measure. (l. 6)

"One should contemplate that which is as beautiful as a half-moon, marked by a single *mātrā* foot, and representing the meaning of the *bindu*. (l. 7)... the connection [of the words] is as follows: "beautiful as a half-moon" means possessing the splendor of a half-moon; this arrangement (*prastāra*) is equal to a half-moon and should be known as the means for accomplishing these two arrangements of five splendors. "Marked by a single *mātrā* foot" means that of a *mātrā*, i.e., a single *mātrā*, there is one foot, one part, namely a fourth part; it is marked—that is, adorned—by that. (p. 7b, l. 1)

The meaning is that it is joined with a measure of one quarter (*pādamātrā*). The meaning is that one should contemplate the half-bindu as the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*). It should be understood that the four digits beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and ending with the resonance (*nāda*) have not been described here separately because they are [subsumed] within the *bindukalā* as the lords of the causes of the principles (*tattva*) such as the trident (*śūla*). The intention is that the half-moon and the others are contained within the upper part of the *bindukalā*.

Now, by the first word of the fourth verse, *nirodhikalāgni* is [the term]; in the reading *rodhikalāpuroditaruci*, it means that the splendor previously mentioned—namely, the luster of the half-moon—is spread forth in the place of *pāla*. "An eighth part of a *mātrā*" means an eighth portion of a single *mātrā*, which is a duration consisting of one-sixteenth of a [long] unit.

This is what is meant: at the utterance of the syllable *ma*, the duration is half a *kāla*; at the utterance of the *ā* [vowel], it is the duration of a *bindu*; the duration of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is the duration of half of that; and the duration of the *nirodhikā-kalā* should be known as the duration of the *nirodhikā-kalā*. This is the meaning of the *nirodhikā-kalā*. In this form of the triangle, he defines the *nāda* and *nādānta-kalās* by means of the second and third quarters of the two verses: "The sixteen-fold portion of the staff (*daṇḍa*), resembling a jewel;
thereafter, within the aperture of Brahmā, the end of the staff, the *tṛṭi*... [as follows].

"Haṭa... half of that is a hundred," meaning the sixteen-part [measure] is like a jewel; the staff (*daṇḍa*) is behind the aperture of Brahmā, with its face toward the bank and light striking back against it until the end of the staff. "Half of that is a *vitasti*," is the remainder. This is the word-connection (*padayojanā*). "Sixteen-part" means endowed with a single portion of a sixteenth part of the measure (*mātrā*). "Like a jewel" means possessing the luster of a ruby (*māṇikya*). The staff (*daṇḍa*) is the expansion in the form of the staff of the digit of sound (*nādakalā*). This is the meaning.

Subsequently, above the *nādakalā* and within the cavity of Brahman, reaching up to the *brahmarandhra*, there is a portion of that *nāda* measuring one part out of a hundred parts. Its luster resembles the sprout of lightning, a light that rivals the distance of a flash; it attains the state of the *daṇḍāgni* at the end of the *nādakalā*. Furthermore, its form on both sides is like a plow (*halākṛti*) joined with two *bindus*. Regarding this, they say it is like a diagram (*prastāra*): the diagram of the end of *nāda* is like a plow joined with a *bindu* on its right side.

Now, by means of the final quarter of the fourth verse and the first quarter of the fifth verse, [the author] speaks of the lords who are the causes of auspiciousness—namely Ardhacandra, Nirodhin, Nāda, and Nādānta—as previously mentioned: "From the middle, on the ground; from the middle, between the eyebrows; measured by a finger-breadth; having taken up the three principles (*tatva*); the [form] of the crescent moon and so forth... the Blessed One himself in the region of the *īśa*. This means that from the middle between the two eyebrows, measured by a finger-breadth, one should take up the three principles of the fourfold group beginning with the crescent moon (*bindvardhādicatuṣṭaya*).

The word-order of the verse is as follows: "The Blessed One, together with his abode, has himself gone to his own task. From the middle region between the two creeper-like eyebrows—starting from the point of the *bindu*—at a distance measured by eleven finger-breadths (*ekādaśāṅgula*) excluding the *bhava*, the word "a... [refers to] Rudra; for Rudras are eleven, and likewise that number eleven is grasped.

(1.3) ...of the four digits (*kalā*) beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) of the four-footed [state]; of the four digits known as *nirodhin*, *nāda*, and *nādānta*; (1.4) having accepted and adopted these three principles (*tatva*) designated as Sādākhya, Śakti, and Śiva—the Lord himself, the Sovereign of the Abode (*sadeśasvayamīśa*), meaning the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*). (1.5) From the middle of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) is three-quarters of a finger-breadth (*pādonatrayāṅgula*), according to the scripture (*śruti*).

From this statement, beginning from the station of the *bindu* up to the end of the *brahmarandhra*, there are eleven [units]. Thus, the station of the *ardhacandrakalā* is at a distance of three *aṅgulas* less a quarter above the middle of the eyebrows; above that is the station of the *nirodhikalā*; above that is the station of the *nāda*; and above that is the station of the *nādānta*. Each of these occupies a space of three *aṅgulas* less a quarter, such that the total station for the four unripened [kalās] is eleven *aṅgulas*. Now, the measurement of the *aṅgula* is shown: in the human body, which measures ninety-six *aṅgulas*, a quarter [is as follows...]

Having set aside forty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from the end of the *mūlādhāra* [upward], within these forty-eight finger-breadths extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*: From the *mūlādhāra* to the end of the navel is one finger-breadth; this is the locus of *ghoṣa*. From the navel to the heart-lotus is twelve finger-breadths; this is the locus of the *kalā* of *medhā* together with *ghoṣa*. From the heart-lotus to the base of the throat is eight finger-breadths; this is the locus of the *kalā* of *rasa* together with *ghoṣa* and *medhā*. From the base of the throat to the root of the tongue is four finger-breadths.

The *rasakalā* together with *vokamedhā* is the locus of the *kalās*. Beginning from the root of the tongue up to the middle of the eyebrows is two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*), which is the locus of the *bindu*. From the locus of the *bindu* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) is ten finger-breadths; this is to be known as the locus of the *kalās* of *ardhacandra*, *nirodhinī*, *nāda*, and *nādānta*. In total, from the base (*mūla*) to the aperture, it is measured at forty-eight finger-breadths. From the feet to the crown of the head, it is to be known as measuring ninety-six finger-breadths. [This refers to] that which resides in the *mūlādhāra*.

The letter *ha*, which is the seed-syllable of Śiva produced by the sound of the *haṃsa* born from the power of Kuṇḍalinī, [travels] by way of the Suṣumnā path through the digits (*kalā*) beginning with Medhā... once again, being heard as a resonance (*nāda*) near the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), it reaches the "end of resonance" (*nādānta*) right there; having reached the end of resonance near the aperture of Brahmā, one should know that it becomes dissolved within the aperture of Brahmā.

Now, by the second quarter of the fifth verse, he describes the *kalā* of Power (*śakti*). "Therefore... in the space of one finger-breadth, Power is the *kalā* of the *Śāṃśikā*" (*atha tasmāt... mathaikāṅgulapade śaktiḥ kalāśāṃ śika iti*). Now, "therefore" (*atha tasmāt*) means above that; "in the space of one finger-breadth" (*ekāṅgulapade*) refers to the *kalā* of the *Śāṃśikā*, which is the Power (*śakti*). This is the meaning of the construction of the words. Furthermore, "thereafter" (*atha...ni*) means after the determination of the end of Sound (*nādānta*). "Therefrom" (*tasmāt*) means from above, from the upper part of the *brahmabila*. "In the space of one finger-breadth" (*ekāṅgulapade*) means in the place of one finger-breadth. There, the *kalā* of Power (*śaktikalā*), which consists of a portion of one-sixteenth of a *yuta* of the fourfold *śāṃśikā*, is to be meditated upon.

The remainder of her left foot (l. 4) is shaped like a plough marked with side-dots; Śiva, the Lord of Causes, has declared that this consists of four digits (*kalā*) beginning with *Prastārā*, *Śatasūryaprabhā*, and *Śakti*. Thus it should be known.

Now, by the second half of the fifth verse, he describes the three voids (*śūnya*) situated within the nine digits from *Medhā* to *Śakti*, as well as the digit *Vyāpinī*. (l. 6) There are three voids, and above them is the digit *Vāpinī*; then, at a distance of three finger-breadths, there is the digit *Śikhā*, which is twice that size, shaped like a trident accompanied by two dots (*bindu*). Here, [the portion] beginning with *Uḍḍha...* [is described].

The *yojanā* consists of one hundred parts of three *kalās*. Thereafter, above that, at a distance of three *aṅgulas*, there is a form shaped like a trident (*śūla*), twice as long [as the previous], provided with two points and a pair of bindus. For the sake of the cessation of the *vipina*, there are three voids divided into three parts of *kalās* starting from *medhā*; thus, there are three voids. At the conclusion of *medhā*, *rasa*, and *viṣa*, the first void occurs.

The first void (*śūnya*) ceases at the *bindu* in the *bhūmi-rodhinī*; the second void is known to be at the end of the *nāda*, *nādānta*, *śakti*, and *kalā*. The third void is to be understood as being within the excellent *kalā* called *medhādi-kātyā*. Above that, by the reduction of one [unit] for each of the thirty triangles, there is the "void of three voids" (*triśūnya*). According to the statement, "Join that which is beyond the void as the Śaiva," following the description of the *śakti-kalā*, above that—three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) further from the single finger-breadth located above the *brahmarandhra*—is the space measured at three finger-breadths.

In that place, the wise [should understand] it to be double that; again, by the number sixty-four, it is doubled to one hundred and twenty-eight. Its parts are the *śikā* (the crest), which is equal to one part of one hundred and twenty-eight. It has the form of a trident (*śūla*) endowed with a pair of dots (*bindu*). Some say that the dot is the form of the trident, being skilled in the expansion (*prastāra*) of its parts. Having established the pervasive (*vyāpinī*) and the container (*vāpinī*)—this is the remainder—it should be known that its radiance, numbering one thousand, is like that of the unstruck (*anāhata*) seed-syllable.

Now, with the first half of the sixth verse, he defines those of equal measure (*samānakalā*): "Consisting of one hundred and sixty-four lines, having six parts, subtle-limbed, four finger-breadths [in height], and then *samanā*... up to the limit of the six parts. As for the meaning: "Then," that is, immediately after that, "pervasive" (*vyāpinī*) is located four finger-breadths above the *brahmarandhra*, at a distance of four finger-breadths further upward. [The next] part is one finger-breadth... [p. 10b, l. 1].

In the four places, there are six [units] added; the number reaches fifty (half a hundred), ten lines, and two pairs (making fifty-two). In total, this amounts to two hundred and fifty-six. A single part of these two hundred and fifty-six parts is joined with exactly one hundred subtle limbs. This is to be meditated upon as the *samanā* level, according to the statement: "The web of bonds (*pāśajāla*) extends up to *samanā*; beyond that is the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*)," because it is delimited by extremely subtle time and reaches the limit of the power of the bonds (*pāśa-praśakti*). As long as the mind is active, there is attachment to the bonds; when the activity of the mind ceases, then the attainment of the supreme state occurs.
As it is said in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikāratnasaṃgraha*:
"When the mind, having attained its mark in the state beyond [the senses], dissolves away,
then specific cognition departs along with destruction."
In the Sūtasamhitā as well, it is stated:

"Upon the cessation of the activity of the intellect (citta), the Self, having transcended the state of the six sheaths, knows its own self-luminosity; thus one says, 'I was conscious during deep sleep.'"
In the *Siddhāntadīpikā*:
"Having negated existence within non-existence, one should make non-existence one's support;
having made the mindless the mind, one should not think of anything at all."

"I am neither action, nor breath, nor mind, nor intellect, nor desire; I do not exist, nor am I anything else. Through the dissolution of consciousness (*cit*), there is no attainment other than the cessation of consciousness"—this is the truth, O Mother of the Multitudes (*Gaṇāmbikā*). Thus we follow the subject at hand: *samanā* means "together with the mind," and it is synonymous with the term *śamanā*.

Its diagram (*prastāra*) is like the letter *ṭa* situated between twelve dots; it is equal to ten million suns. Now, one should describe the *unmana* stage from the half-measure of the sixth world beyond. [The text] speaks of the Lords of the Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*) among those who are *śātivāpinī*, *sama*, and *unmanā*.

That certain power called Unmanā, which possesses four fingers (caturaṅgula), triumphs; it is the beloved power of the Lord within the fourfold group of powers. [The phrase] "having destroyed Śiva" refers to the light of ten million [suns]. Thus, in the place of four fingers above the eight fingers, having gone upward from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), it resides above the opening of the powers and so forth, according to the statement: "the space above the opening is four fingers [measured by] the Vedas and the Yugas."

The meaning is that she measures eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) above the *uparatanu* [cakra]. From the *kalpa*, she possesses the radiance of ten million suns; she is the dissolution of *yojanas*. Struck by the brilliance of ten million suns, she is named *Unmanā*—she from whom the mind (*manas*) has departed. She is established as being called *Unmanā*; she is the bestower of the cessation of mental activity. O Lord, she is a certain power (*śakti*) of Paramaśiva, possessing infinite flavor, renowned, and victorious—she exists as something transcendent. Indeed, because the mind belongs to the twenty-fourth principle within the *ātmatattva*.

If it is asked: "How can the state of *unmanā* belong to the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), which exists transcending the seven principles of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*), the five principles of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*), and the powers of will, knowledge, and action, as well as the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*)?"—it is said in reply:

The principle of Īśvara is the effect of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*); the principle of Śuddhavidyā is [the effect of the power of knowledge]; and the principle of Śakti is the effect of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Furthermore, within the manifestation of the principle of Īśvara, there is the operation of the principle of Rāga; within the manifestation of the principle of Śuddhavidyā, there is the operation of the principle of Vidyā; and within the manifestation of the principle of Śakti, there is the operation of the principle of Kalā. Moreover, from the principle of Rāga, there is the operation of the principle of Manas; from the principle of Aśuddhavidyā, there is the operation of the principle of Buddhi; and from the principle of Kalā, there is the operation of the principle of Ahaṅkāra.

And thus, through its conjunction with the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), it is the pervasive activity of the Self; this is the meaning of all [the preceding]. Therefore, since all the principles (*tattvas*) are the effects of the action of cognition, they are established therein as being equal to what was stated in the core of our own doctrine regarding the nature of the will-power (*icchā-śakti*) of the mind. As for the statement: "The mind, whose nature is will, is that which—moving swiftly as the cause for the engagement of the senses with their objects—constantly performs as if it were volition, producing the maintenance [of the body]. If this is said:

Because of the statement, "The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) arises from a thousandth part of the power of the Supreme (*parā-śakti*)," it follows that the cessation of the powers of knowledge and action has been established. Therefore, when the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*), whose nature is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), comes to rest, it is logical that the powers of action and knowledge also come to rest; thus, the powers of will, knowledge, and action would not arise [again]. Because of the statement, "The power of knowledge arises from a thousandth part of the power of will, and the power of action arises from a thousandth part of the power of knowledge," [the power of] knowledge...

Since desire alone is the cause of action, when that causal power of desire is stilled, there is also the stilling of the effects—the powers of knowledge and action; thus, there is no fault. Therefore, it has been stated that in the absence of [desire], there is indeed the absence of knowledge and action. Now, if it is asked, "In the absence of knowledge, how can there be the activity of desire?"—this is true.

Through knowledge (*jñāna*), will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*) [are contained]; through will, knowledge and action; and through action, knowledge and will. Thus, the mutual inclusion of the three powers (*śakti-traya*) is indeed the very intention of all the scriptures (*sakalāgama*). Nevertheless, how is it that the powers of will, knowledge, and action are included within the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), whose nature consists of existence, bliss, and knowledge? Because of the proximity of the supreme power, whose essential nature is unfragmented knowledge of sound (*nādakhaṇḍa-jñāna*), it is first stated that knowledge belongs to the power of will itself.

It has been stated that when the power of will (*icchāśakti*) comes to rest, there is the cessation of all principles (*sarvatattva*). Thus it is said: "At the end of *unmanā* is Supreme Śiva" (*unmanyante paraśśivam*). Following the sequence of what is desired and so forth, within the fourfold group of powers previously established—namely the four powers called *vyāpinī*, *samana*, and *unmanā*—Śiva is the Unstruck (*anāhata*), the agent of the principle of Śiva, who is the Lord of Causes; this is the remaining sense. The nature of the twelve digits (*kalā*) is now described: the mind, or rather the supreme tranquility, is the digit of *unmanā*, which is Śiva.
When the activity of the mind has become tranquil for one whose nature is the self, and yet mental activity still occurs, then there is the experience of the *samanā-kalā*.

1) In the state where the mind has reached its limit (*vāpti*), there is the experience of the *vāpti-kalā*, which is the power of exertion in the utterance of the mantra. At that moment, there is the emergence of the *śakti-kalā*. (l. 2) At the onset of *nāda*, there is the experience of the *nāda-kalā*. In the form of the cessation of conceptualization, at the conclusion of the mantra during the contemplation of the sound being heard, there is the experience of the *nāda-kalā*. (l. 3) On the occasion of the third part of the utterance of the *bindu*, there is the experience of the *nirodhinī-kalā*.

By the emission from the upper half of the *bindu*, there is the experience of the crescent digit (*ardhacandra-kalā*) at the fringe (*daśā*). At the very moment of the meditative conjunction (*anusandhāna*) of the *bindu* uttered above the poison-digit (*viṣa-kalā*), there is the experience of the *bindu*-digit; immediately thereafter, by the utterance of the letter *ma*, there is the experience of the poison-digit.

By the utterance of the vowel *ū*, there is the experience of the *rasa*-kalā; by the utterance of the vowel *au*, there is the experience of the *medhā*-kalā. Thus, regarding the time of emanation (*sṛṣṭikāla*), how is it stated that starting from the *unmanā* [state], each subsequent kalā is produced from the preceding kalā? It is said that Brahman, who is the Lord (*īśvara*) and the cause of *medhā*, is produced from the syllable *ru*; Viṣṇu, the cause of *rasa*, is produced from the syllable *vi*; Rudra, the cause of *viṣa*, is produced from the syllable *ru*; Maheśvara, the cause of the *bindu*, is produced from Rudra, the cause of *viṣa*; and [Maheśvara] is the cause of the *bindu*.

The state of being created by Īśvara and Sadāśiva, who are the causes of the Half-moon, the Obstructress, and the End of Sound. [The cause of the Half-moon, the Obstructress, and the End of Sound] (p.13a, l.1).

There is no fault in [the claim that] Sadāśiva possesses the state of being the object of creation for the unstruck sound (*anāhata-śiva*), who is the Lord of the causes in the forms of *samana* and *unmanā*, which pervade the power (*śakti*). Now, the method of dissolution is described: the letter *ha*, the seed-syllable of Śiva consisting of vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature is will and which is composed of the mantra of recitation produced by the *kuṇḍalinī* power residing in the *mūlādhāra*, pervades as far as the lotus of the navel in the form of the letter *ha*. Subsequently, it pervades up to the root of the throat in the form of the letters *ha*, *au*, and *ū*.

Thereafter, there is pervasion as far as the palate by means of the two *ū* sounds. (l. 4) Through the conjunction with the *bindu*, there is pervasion as far as the center of the eyebrows. At the time of the upward emission of the *bindu*, there is the pervasion of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). At the time of the cessation of the *bindu*, (l. 5) there is pervasion in the *nirodhinī*. Thus, from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *nirodhinī*, there is the application of the *kalā* imagined through the recitation of mantra for the subtle resonance (*nāda*) arising from the *mūlādhāra*. Thereafter, there is the sound (*nāda*) which is self-cognizable in its subtlety.

Following its cessation, there is dissolution in the region of the *brahmarandhra*, the locus of the end of sound (*nādānta*). Immediately after the dissolution of sound, the digit of the end of sound (*nādāntakalā*) merges into the digit of the causal power (*kāraṇaśaktikalā*). Within the digit that pervades the digit of power, the digit of pervasive power (*vyāpinīkalā*) [merges] into the digit of equalization (*samanā*).

I too, through the experience of the *unmanā-kalā*, become the *unmanā-kalā*. The mantra is inscribed within the *unmanā-kalā*; having abandoned the twenty-six principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, which arise at that moment, one attains the Supreme (*parā*) by means of Will, Knowledge, and Action. Having abandoned even the aspects of Knowledge and Action and having realized the yoga of the Supreme, when one abides [therein], that is the experience of the *unmanā-kalā*. At that time, there is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Paramaśiva, whose nature is supreme bliss.

Let us follow the subject at hand. Thus, regarding the description of the ten *kalās*: the teacher, the mantra-master, does not say that one who intends to construct a temple (*prāsāda*) endowed with sixteen *kalās* (twice eight) undergoes fruitless toil in the rite, because of the statement [to the contrary]. Furthermore, a temple of sixteen *kalās* is also observed; for by conceiving a tetrad of *kalās*—namely, *Vyomarūpā*, *Anantā*, *Anāthā*, and *Anāśritā*—situated above *Vyāpinī* and below *Samanā*, there comes to be a state of sixteen *kalās* within *Vyāpinī*, which resides within *Samanā*.

According to the statement, "In that which is called Vyomāṅga-ananta, there are eight kalās joined with the two [states] of being without protector and without support; this is Śiva," and according to the statement, "Now, the *samaya* [kalās] are all [the others]; the twenty-five special ones constitute the group of eight," the *prāsāda* mantras consisting of five kalās and eight kalās are described. Among these, the five kalās are as stated in the *Siddhāntarahasya*:
"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*;
and the letter *ha*, which is the transformation of the *siddhi*—these are called the five kalās."

"Śiva is indeed the eightfold [syllable] consisting of the vowel *au*, the eight parts, the bindu, the circle (*vṛtta*), the half-sound (*nādaka*), and joined with Śakti and Samanā. Here too, it should be understood that the letter *ha* undergoes a modification through sandhi.

Thus, the descriptions of the characteristics of the temple with eight *kalās*, including the manifestation of its states (*avasthā*) and so forth, are written here. As for the states: the utterance of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the waking state; the dream state is the *bindu*... [the deep sleep state is] from the union with *nāda*; and the fourth state (*turya*) is the gathering of that energy (*śakti*). The descriptions of the characteristics of the manifestation of the states of this *nāda* and so forth are written here. As for the states: the utterance of the seed-syllable is the waking state; the dream state is the *bindu*... [the deep sleep state is] from the union with *nāda*; and the fourth state is the gathering of that energy.

"The place of dissolution is said to be the Supreme Light (*mahasi*) at the end of the Fourth (*turyānta*). Thus [ends the section on] pronunciation. (l. 4) Having known the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, the agent should perform what is desired. The gross is declared to be "sound" (*śabda*); the subtle would consist of thought (*cintāmaya*). That which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme. (l. 5) Thus, there is a threefold pronunciation according to the divisions of *āṇava*, *śākta*, and *śāmbhava*. The *āṇava* [pronunciation], which is appropriate for the resonance (*nāda*) arising from the locus of meditation, consists of those mantras consisting of thought. (l. 6) Those [mantras]...

The Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Cit are the threefold gross [forms], consisting of the elemental (*ādhibhautika*), the intermediate form (*ādhyākṛtika*), and the divine (*ādhidaivika*). One should exclude the full form; that which ends with the subtle is called "sound" (*śabda*). One should proclaim it as being endowed with the pride of phonemes (*varṇa*) and the principles (*tattva*). Through expansion (*prastāra*), extension (*vistāra*), spreading (*vistāra*), and dissolution (*staimitya*), it manifests the five states of the phonemes (*varṇa*). In that regard, *prastāra* is by means of drawing the forms of the parts (*kalā*), the triangle, the plow, the trident, and so forth. Now, *vistāra* is below... [end of fragment].

The expansion of the mantras—their manifestation within the seven wombs such as the *liṅga*, the *aṅga*, and the *bera*, as well as in the paths (*adhvan*) and the terrestrial realm (*adhibhauma*), and in the internal (*adhyātma*)—is the mind. Their deliverance (*nistāra*) occurs through their nature as five, eight, and twelve *kalās*, consisting of short, long, and protracted vowels; this is established by the statement: "Those four [vowels] follow in sequence. Furthermore, it is said: "Neither waking nor dreaming, nor the state beyond dreams, nor the perception of sounds, but that which is beyond, pure consciousness alone, free from rejection and grasping"—this is the contemplation (*anusandhāna*).

Now, having understood that the activity of both mind and eye is like the moon and the sun, [one realizes] that when the moon and sun have perished, sacrifice is the supreme means for accomplishing all siddhis. Regarding the five states of the utterance (*uccāraṇa*), it is as follows: the gross sound-measure attains the state of the *bindu*, and that too becomes composed of *nāda*.

Even the power (*śakti*) that remains abides through dissolution (*laya*) in that state of consciousness (*cit*); this non-differentiation from dissolution is *prasāda*. Now, regarding the pervasiveness (*vyāpinī*) of the self, mantra, channel (*nāḍī*), and power, the nature of *samanā* is as follows: situated in the seventh stage known as *samanā*, just as the mantra of the Equal Taste (*samarasa*) is first to be known within the self, the second is [the mantra] designated as the channel; thereafter, the third is in the power (*śakti*), and the fourth is in the place of the pervasive (*vyāpinī*). The fifth is in the activity of *samanā*... the goddess is the Equal Taste (*samarasa*).

The seventh [stage], however, is prescribed as follows: having grasped the disciple’s self according to the previously mentioned method, one should subsequently join it with one’s own self. One should contemplate the state of *lolī-* [fusion]. Having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should restrain the breath along with the *samana* wind. Then, having uttered the mantra, one should contemplate it as dissolved into the resonance (*nāda*). This is the nature of the mantra.

And likewise, the *nāḍī* [channel] becomes thus of equal flavor (*samarasa*). Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself—therefore, the *nāda* should emerge until it has gone to dissolution within the *śakti*. Having entered the midst of the *śakti*, the Self is established as the *nāda*. The entire *tantra* consists of all powers; everything becomes of equal flavor. Above that, having pervaded the *vyāpinī*, one should attain identity with her. Above that, having reached the *samanā*, one should again attain identity with her.

Having reached the path, one should abide in the state of *samarasa* (equilibrium) with Brahman; wherever the mind goes, one should contemplate that very object of knowledge as the "End" (*tatraiva*). Thus is *samarasa* proclaimed, which is the equinox (*viṣuva*) for the wise who have attained awakening. ...Now, regarding the measures of the channels of mantra, the characteristics of the seven equinoxes known as *praśānta-śakti*, *kāla*, and *manas*, the measures are as follows:

The *pramāṇa*, the *mantra*, the *nāḍī*, the *praśānta*, the *śakti*, the *kāla*, the *naśa*, and the *vikumba*—the differentiation of these is called the *ātman*. Having joined the mind (*manaḥ*) with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it becomes the *viṣuva*; one should utter the *mantra* until one becomes free from mental distraction (*ekāgra*). Among all the *nāḍīs*, that which is situated on the left is named *suṣumnā*; this *nāḍī* of Śakti reaches Śiva by means of Śakti. Causing the resonance (*nāda*) to flow therein, it is called the *viṣuva-nāḍī*.

This should be known as tranquil and pleasing, the range of the senses being tranquil; it should be known as stilled and motionless, the sign being steady and firm. Within the sixteen bodies of the visions, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established in peace. Having made the vital breath thus threefold in time, one should likewise abandon it again. Standing above the other power, [it is] within the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*).

The second and third [stages] are said to be the equinox (*viṣuva*) in the state of *samanā*. There, one should unite the self with the Goddess Unmanā. One who is thus joined therein and from whom the self is born—having understood the equinox according to the rule—is released from bondage. Thus, having thoroughly examined this commentary on the eight verses of the *Prāsāda* written by me, O wise ones, who would not be called released from bondage? Salutation to Śiva.

From the root, from the abode of her residence, Śiva dwells within the navel like a sprout of light lasting for a moment of the *u* vowel, resembling the cry of a swan amidst lotuses. Above that, at a distance of one span (*vitasti*), is the heart-lotus measuring four fingers; there, the flame of fire has blossomed, and above that, she who is flooded with wisdom has attained [her place]. O Lord seated upon the lotus-throne, among the twenty-four principles, you are marked by the two measures (*mātrā*) of the moon’s radiance at the throat, which measures eight fingers.

One should remember the Person (Puruṣa), accompanied by the six principles (tattvas) and joined with Lakṣmī, marked by a measure of one-sixteenth of a digit (kalā) on the tongue at a distance of four digits; [he who is] as brilliant as a flash of lightning, the father of the world, accompanied by Māyā, located there at two digits, resembling the flame of a lamp between the eyebrows, joined with half a measure, conjoined with the two principles (Sattva and Rajas), and possessing the Bindu, which is the Vidyā-born Intellect (Buddhi), shining like the moon when offered as an oblation (arghya).

How could one describe the single-footed [state] arising from the mass of the *rodhika* syllables, which possesses the luster of the eighth part of a measure? With a staff of sixteen parts, resembling a sapphire, and having the brilliance of a lightning-flash at its tip that rivals the sprout of a lotus-stalk, the Lord himself, from the midst of the hundred [parts], having accepted the three principles (*tattva*) starting from the point (*bindu*) above the four-footed [base]—measured by the fingers of the earth’s creeper—from that [point] upwards, in the space of one finger-breadth, there is the power (*śakti*) consisting of a portion of a sixteenth part; then the voids consist of a portion of three sixteenths.

Above that is Vyāpinī, one finger-breadth in extent; behind her is Śakti, twice that size, having the form of a trident marked with two dots and endowed with six peaks. Beyond that, the remaining Śakti, subtle-limbed and measuring four finger-breadths, extending as far as the attachment to the noose of Samanā, triumphs along with its power; it is the certain Unmanā named Śakti of the Lord. When the four powers are struck, Śiva, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, is awakened from his state of dissolution.

"Kāla" refers to the six-verse [section]; it is the lotus with twelve petals, each having four time-units (*kalā*), the abode of splendor, where the Kuṇḍalinī—whose sound is like a serpent coiled at the root of the channels and whose limbs are the vows—resides.
Therefore, seated within that, he who possesses a universal form shines like a river.
Four finger-breadths above the navel, at the end of a span, is the heart;
situated at its end is this [energy] with the radiance of the crest of a flame from the water-born fire.
The cause consists of three measures and is joined with the twenty-four principles of Brahman;
at the throat, within eight finger-breadths, it is purified by the measure of three and possesses the luster of the moon.
Viṣṇu, endowed with the six principles (*tattva*), is at the palate four finger-breadths [above];
the principle of Amāyā is poison, and Rudra is a single *mātrā* with the luster of lightning.
Two finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows is [the letter] resembling a lamp-flame, measuring half a circle;
at the forehead, two *tattvas* joined with Ananta, it measures one quarter.
In the half-verse, the lunar light obstructs the eight measures and the directions;
the lord of jewels is the sixteenth part of the arm-staff of the aforementioned dawn.
The thirty-second [part] is at the end of the staff, possessing the brilliance of lightning in the aperture.
From the point above the eyebrows up to the opening, there are one hundred and eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
At the top of the power of the *śikhā*, sixty-four [finger-breadths] are situated at one *aṅgula*.
At three *aṅgulas*, the *vyāpinī* consists of one hundred and twenty-eight *śikhās*.
The śikhā consists of twenty-five [units], joined with four aṅgulas and six [units];
it is equal above, measuring one mātrā of the mind, and slightly exceeding four aṅgulas.
Beyond that is the Supreme Measure (Paramamātra), who transcends the principles (tattva) and is the Supreme Śiva;
he is like a stainless tooth in appearance and possesses a luster like autumnal water—
He is to be reached by this very sequence through the self-experience of the Great-Souled One.
The sound *nāda* is said to be the crown; *bindu* is declared to be the face. The letter *ha* is explained as the heart, and the letter *ū* as the two arms.
The sixth is the pair of feet, which is the Vidyā; Sadāśiva is the embodiment of the mantra.
(l.2) Holding the auspicious [trident] with one eye, he is the supreme Śiva, peaceful, and composed of fifteen [parts].
The entire sphere of existence, supreme and manifest, whose nature is Rudra, consists of the two syllables of Jambhāri; it is the fourth Veda, consisting of the supreme state.
May this supreme mantra, which contains all seeds within itself, be for the welfare of Śiva.

May there be auspiciousness. (L.4) The word *ca* [is used] in the sense of "and"; that which perceives all arts at the place of birth—O Knower, may we know that very sound which was spoken by You as *śabda*. (L.5) A mind free from agitation is pure Śiva; it becomes its own universal life-force. Beyond that, even gold... (L.6) a bed of flowers is not required. Birth is the abode of memory, free from desire for the three worlds. ॥ Śubham ॥
